deep_batch1.py.quoted_phrase: allows engineers to plot direct wave paths as straight lines rather than calculating path curvature explicitly
deep_batch1.py.description: This string is inside quotation marks and introduced as the ITU's own words ("The ITU's own handbook is explicit about what the trick is for"), but it does not occur in ITU-R Handbook R-HDB-54. The handbook, §3.3 'Diffraction fading and path clearance', reads: 'To avoid having to calculate the path curvature when designing a link, the effective Earth radius can be used instead of the actual Earth radius. In this modified geometry, the difference between the path of the direct wave and the Earth's curvature becomes constant and the path of the direct wave can be plotted as a straight line, helping to identify possible obstructions by the terrain profile or Earth's surface.' The substance of our claim is correct; the quotation is a paraphrase wearing quotation marks. On a site whose entire product is that claims degrade in transmission, publishing our own paraphrase as a verbatim quote is the single most discreditable error available to us, and it is trivially found by anyone who Ctrl-Fs the cited PDF.
deep_batch1.py.recommendation: Replace the quoted clause and its frame with: The ITU’s own handbook says why the trick exists: “To avoid having to calculate the path curvature when designing a link, the effective Earth radius can be used instead of the actual Earth radius. In this modified geometry … the path of the direct wave can be plotted as a straight line.” That is the same move as balanced backsights — curvature folded into the coordinate frame so the drawing looks straight.

deep.py.quoted_phrase: On a stationary Earth there is no relative velocity between source and observer, so there is no aberration to have a magnitude at all.
deep.py.description: scripts/deep.py:146. The refutation's third step — the one our own text calls fatal — attacks a naive stationary-Earth model in which nothing moves. Van der Kamp's model has the starry dome revolving relative to a resting Earth, so relative velocity is present and he does have an account of aberration. A defender opens De Labore Solis at p. 40 and reads 'the Earth is at rest relative to space ... then the starry dome is revolving relative to us', notes the chapter at p. 19 titled 'Geocentric? Heliocentric? The Janus-faced Aberration Can't Tell', and adds Bouw's obituary line that 'Walter believed [aberration] implied a small universe 60 light days in radius'. Our sentence is then visibly false of the source, our claim that 'this is the step the argument never takes' is visibly false, and the section reads as a debunk of a position nobody defends. He can do this using two of the six links we ourselves publish. The same error is carried at the highest-visibility point on the page, in the TLDR phrase 'aberration exists at all only because the Earth moves', and in the ARG-A03 basis line in scripts/clusters.py, 'Aberration existing at all is itself evidence Earth moves.'
deep.py.recommendation: Replace the third paragraph's middle with: "Stellar aberration is the annual ~20.5-arcsecond elliptical wobble Bradley discovered in 1729, and it is produced by the observer's motion, not the source's — a star's own velocity shifts where it appears only through light-travel time, which is why every star shows the same aberration constant regardless of its distance or its proper motion (de Sitter's binary-star argument, 1913). Van der Kamp saw the problem and paid for it. His geocentric account keeps aberration by having the starry dome revolve around a resting Earth, and to keep the dome's tangential speed below c he had to shrink the universe: Bouw's obituary records that 'Walter believed [aberration] implied a small universe 60 light days in radius.' That is the price of the model, and it is the refutation. In a revolving-dome cosmos the aberration angle would be the star's tangential speed over c, so it would grow with distance without limit; observed aberration is flat at 20.5 arcseconds for the nearest star and the most distant quasar alike, which is what observer motion predicts and what source motion cannot. A 60-light-day universe is also excluded by the parallaxes Gaia DR3 publishes for ~1.468 billion sources. The argument takes an experiment that measures a consequence of the Earth's orbital motion, shows the magnitude is medium-independent, and reports this as evidence the Earth does not move." Change the TLDR's closing clause to "and the aberration it measures is produced by the observer's motion, which is why the geocentric version of the argument needs a universe 60 light-days across." Make the matching change to the clusters.py basis line.

_b6_A05.py.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:224 (and TLDR line 51, gloss line 94, steelman line 167, verdict line 339, docstring line 36). Our load-bearing charge - that Rowbotham asserts the three-foot base line "as the result of actual experiment" and then supplies no experiment - is contradicted by the same chapter of the same edition we quote and link. Evidence: sacred-texts za21.htm, pp. 79-81, seven pages before our own quoted p. 86: "Take two carefully-bored metallic tubes, not less than six feet in length, and place them one yard asunder, on the opposite sides" of a wooden frame, axes adjusted so they "shall be perfectly parallel to each other", directed at "some notable fixed star, a few seconds previous to its meridian time", an observer at each tube - "The moment the star appears in the tube A, T, let a loud knock or other signal be given, to be repeated by the observer at the tube B, T, when he first sees the same star" - with the stated result that "a distinct period of time will elapse between the signals given", i.e. the star "is not visible at the same moment by two parallel lines of sight...when only one yard asunder". One yard IS three feet; the p. 86 sentence is a back-reference to that experiment, not a bare assertion. So "No apparatus" is simply false, and the same false claim carries into the two fields a skimming reader actually sees: the TLDR ("the right discriminating test, asserted with no experiment attached") and the verdict paragraph ("was published without an experiment"), plus the gloss ("an experiment he does not describe") and the steelman ("he offers no observation for it"). What survives is narrower and needs saying separately: he names no star, no date, no observer and no measured angle. The damaging part is that the true refutation is stronger than ours - the apparatus exists and cannot possibly measure the quantity in dispute, so what it detects is its own construction error.
_b6_A05.py.recommendation: Replace "No experiment follows. No apparatus, no star, no date, no observer, no number." with: "He does supply an experiment, and it is the weak point. Seven pages earlier, at pp. 79-81, he sets out the apparatus: two bored metallic tubes at least six feet long, fixed “one yard asunder” on a wooden frame with their axes made “perfectly parallel,” sighted on a bright star near meridian transit by two observers who knock when the star enters their tube. His reported result is that “a distinct period of time will elapse between the signals given.” That is the three-foot base line of p. 86. It is also the whole problem. Two genuinely parallel tubes one yard apart, sighted on a star, must show it simultaneously: the real parallax over one yard is 1.7 × 10<sup>−12</sup> arcsec, while a naked eye behind a six-foot tube resolves no better than about a minute of arc — some ten orders of magnitude coarser. A lag between the two knocks therefore measures one thing only: the residual angle between the two tubes’ axes, with the star’s diurnal drift of roughly 15 arcsec per second of time converting that misalignment into a delay he can hear. He built an instrument that reads out its own construction error and recorded the reading as a stellar parallax. He names no star, no date, no observer and no measured angle, and describes no null-alignment control. The experiment is real; what it detects is the frame." Then fix the four downstream instances: TLDR line 51 to "— the right discriminating test — and he backed it with two six-foot tubes set a yard apart, an instrument ten orders of magnitude too coarse to run it."; gloss lines 94-95 to "he answers them with an experiment whose apparatus cannot resolve the angle in dispute"; steelman line 167 to "and the only observation he offers for it is a pair of hand-aligned tubes"; verdict line 339 to "is wrong by eleven orders of magnitude, and the experiment offered for it measures the alignment of his own tubes."

Set drift_type="hedge_dropped" and replace the note's opening paragraph with: "

The dominant drift is a qualifier doing no work. Items 5, 37 and 264 keep their scope — early measurements, naked-eye parallax — and as written are simply true; what changes is that a scoped historical observation is entered as a numbered proof of a stationary Earth, where the reader supplies the generalisation the sentence withholds. Note what the list does not do: no item here denies that parallax is measured. That denial appears downstream, in Dubay’s proof 19 — “not a single inch of parallax can be detected in the stars, proving we have not moved at all” — which is a straight reversal of Rowbotham, who prints 0″.98 and 0″.35. It also appeared in the name we first gave this cluster. We have renamed it; a summary title that overstates the items it summarises is the same fault we are documenting.

" Rename the cluster at scripts/clusters.py:46 from "No measurable stellar parallax" to "Stellar parallax reassigned to a three-foot base line", and change the TLDR opening (line 47) from "The cluster is titled “no measurable stellar parallax” and its own source prints the measurements" to "This cluster reads as a denial that parallax is measurable. deep_batch3.py.description: Wrong by a factor of two, and it conflates two different quantities in a paragraph whose whole job is to show we know the physics. The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ωsinφ, correctly stated earlier in the same refutation ("The strength of the deflection is f = 2Ωsinφ"). The precession rate of a Foucault pendulum's plane of swing is Ωsinφ — half of f. Confirmed against the standard statement of the pendulum's precession rate and rotation period (Wikipedia, Foucault pendulum: rate = Ω sin φ, full turn in ~32 h at the latitude of Paris; the 2Ωsinφ figure would give ~16 h, which is not what the Paris pendulum did). This is the single most screenshot-able error in the entry: a defender does not need to know any meteorology to use it, only the pendulum formula, and it sits in the paragraph headed "Routine measurement" where we are asserting our own rigour.
deep_batch3.py.recommendation: Foucault demonstrated rotation directly in Paris on 3 February 1851, and the demonstration is quantitative: the plane of swing precesses at Ωsinφ — half the Coriolis parameter — so a full turn takes about 32 hours at the latitude of Paris, slows towards the equator, and never completes there at all.

deep_batch2.py.quoted_phrase: every one of them is true

deep_batch2.py.quoted_phrase: matching 2Ωsinφ at the latitude of Paris
deep_batch2.py.description: Factual physics error. A Foucault pendulum's plane precesses at Ω sin φ, not 2Ω sin φ. 2Ω sin φ is the Coriolis parameter f and is exactly twice the pendulum rate. Our own numbers prove the formula wrong in the same sentence: 15.041°/hr × sin 48.87° = 11.33°/hr, which matches the '11.3° per hour' we quote; 2Ω sin φ would give 22.7°/hr. Confirmed against Wikipedia's Foucault pendulum article, which gives 'ω = Ω sin φ' and the same 28 kg bob, 67 m wire and 11.3°/hr for the Panthéon (those three are correct as written). This is the single cheapest shot available to a physically literate defender: our marquee rotation experiment, stated with a formula that disagrees with our own number by a factor of two.
deep_batch2.py.recommendation: Replace 'matching 2Ωsinφ at the latitude of Paris' with 'matching Ωsinφ at the latitude of Paris'.

deep_batch2.py.quoted_phrase: They do not cite GPS. They do not cite WGS 84, ITRF, seismic hypocentres or a nautical almanac. In the whole of the passage this cluster rests on, no instrument is named at all, and Sungenis’s own later restatements of the case reach for the same Einstein sentence without naming one.
deep_batch2.py.description: Both flat sentences are false of the work, and the final clause is false outright. Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II ch. 10 contains a subsection headed "Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses" (p. 204 of its own contents list, archive.org scan ...Bennett4276), and the same volume discusses GPS signal timing and the Sagnac effect at length. More damagingly, Sungenis's 2010 reply to Phil Plait of Discover Magazine (isidore.co, Sungenis & DeLano folder) makes precisely the R08 argument while naming the instrument: "Using the ECI frame (Earth Centered Inertial Frame) is much easier than the Solar Barycentric frame. If you don't believe me I suggest you ask the engineers who put up the GPS." That is a later restatement of the case that names an instrument, which is what we say does not exist. Since this paragraph is the premise of the whole second half of the refutation ("The twenty-eight items are the list's addition, not the authors'") and of the compression verdict, a defender who owns the books discredits the section with one page reference. Same error class as corrections.json entries 4 and 11: asserting absence from a source on the strength of one passage.
deep_batch2.py.recommendation: They do not cite GPS in it, or WGS 84, ITRF, seismic hypocentres or a nautical almanac: in the whole of the passage this cluster rests on, no instrument is named at all. Elsewhere they do, and it should be said plainly. Vol. II, ch. 10 carries a subsection headed “Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses”, and Sungenis’s 2010 reply to Phil Plait of Discover argues that “Using the ECI frame (Earth Centered Inertial Frame) is much easier than the Solar Barycentric frame. If you don’t believe me I suggest you ask the engineers who put up the GPS.” So a handful of these items — the GPS and ECI ones — do have an ancestor in the authors’ own writing, and we withdraw any suggestion otherwise. What that sentence claims is ease of use. It does not claim fixity, and the twenty or so remaining artefacts are not in the books at all. The gap between “easier to compute in” and “therefore at rest” is the whole of this cluster, and it is the list that closes it, not Sungenis.

_b6_B01.py.quoted_phrase: It never meant “planar” and was never derived from geometry
_b6_B01.py.description: False, and it contradicts our own steelman two fields earlier. Etymonline gives the adjective 'level' as 'having an even surface' from early 15c. and 'lying in the same horizontal plane (as something else)' from the 1550s — three centuries before Rowbotham. Our steelman concedes exactly this ('In ordinary English a level line is a straight horizontal one') and calls the complaint fair. A defender needs one dictionary lookup to catch us asserting in the refutation what we grant in the steelman, on the single lexical point the whole section turns on. The true and sufficient claim is about priority, not about non-existence.
_b6_B01.py.recommendation: It began as the name of the instrument that finds the direction of gravity, not as a term of geometry; the planar senses are later derivations from it — the adjective “having an even surface” is attested only from the early fifteenth century, and “lying in the same horizontal plane” from the 1550s, two centuries after the tool. An argument that runs “we say sea level, not sea curve” leans on the derived sense while presenting it as the original one, and the original one names a gravity instrument.

_b6_B04.py.quoted_phrase: Four of his hundred proofs are in this cluster and none of them is in Rowbotham.
_b6_B04.py.description: False as to proof 63, and on a provenance site a false negative about ancestry is the error class corrections.json already logs three times (C02, B01, R06). Rowbotham 1881 ch. XIV (sacred-texts za33.htm) contains the telescope claim directly: "But even on the sea, when the water is very calm, if a vessel is observed until it is just 'hull down,' a powerful telescope turned upon it will restore the hull to sight." The same chapter reports the Nab light-ship hull "through a good telescope, plainly visible" from 32 inches at eight miles. Worse, the correction is against our own interest twice over: it strengthens the lineage, and Rowbotham's version carries a condition Carpenter drops. Rowbotham also writes "In the case of a ship's hull a telescope fails to restore it, however powerful it may be" when the sea is running; Carpenter's proof 63 states the effect unconditionally and the TFES wiki still does ("a good telescope with sufficient zoom will change the observer's perspective and bring the ship's hull back in full view" — verified verbatim). That is a hedge_dropped on a falsifiable claim, the best specimen in the cluster, and neither the gloss nor the compression note mentions it.
_b6_B04.py.recommendation: Four of his hundred proofs are in this cluster. The Cape Hatteras figure and the two Chesapeake cases are his own and are nowhere in Rowbotham; the telescope claim is not. Rowbotham had already written it, with a condition attached: “even on the sea, when the water is very calm, if a vessel is observed until it is just ‘hull down,’ a powerful telescope turned upon it will restore the hull to sight” (ch. XIV), while in a running sea “a telescope fails to restore it, however powerful it may be”. Proof 63 states the same effect with the condition removed, and the Flat Earth Society wiki still repeats it that way. The hedge that was dropped here is the one that made the claim survivable.

_b6_B04.py.quoted_phrase: about a seventh of the 491-foot curvature term, some 70 feet
_b6_B04.py.description: 491 feet is not the curvature term. It is the curvature drop less the light's own altitude, which is how every figure in Rowbotham's table is built, and his own printed results prove it: Egero, 28 statute miles less a 4-mile observer horizon is 24; 8 in x 24^2 = 384 ft; 384 less the light's 154 ft = 230 ft, which is exactly the depression Dubay's proof 83 reprints. Bonavista: 35 less 4 is 31; 8 in x 31^2 = 641 ft; 641 less 150 = the 491 he prints. Cordonan and Port Nicholson reconstruct the same way. So the curvature term is about 641 feet, one-seventh of it is about 90 feet rather than 70, a one-fifth day takes about 130 rather than "more than 90", and the sentence four lines later, "the allowance he made was five times too small", should be about seven times. Getting the arithmetic wrong in the paragraph headed "The source contains the correction. This is the finding." is the most expensive place on the page to get it wrong. (Related: the gloss's "Allowing 16 feet ... 5 miles must be taken from the 30 miles" is genuine but belongs to the Spurn Point coal-fire example, not to the lighthouse table, where he uses the 10-foot standard and the 4-mile horizon reconstructed above.)
_b6_B04.py.recommendation: on Cape Bonavista he deducts 13 feet from a curvature term of about 641 feet — his printed 491 is that 641 less the light's own 150 feet, as the rest of his table confirms: Egerö, 28 miles less a 4-mile horizon, squared, times 8 inches, is 384 feet, and 384 less 154 is the 230 he gives — where the encyclopaedia's own mean would take about a seventh of the 641, some 90 feet, and a strong-refraction day nearer 130. Change the following sentence to read: the allowance he made was about seven times too small and applied to the wrong variable.

_b7_C04.py.quoted_phrase: and we have no evidence that he did
_b7_C04.py.description: We assert we have no evidence Skiba took the proof-text set from Schadewald. The evidence is inside the very document we quote as our passage. Skiba's "The Bible and the Still Flat Earth" (the 2015-2016 PDF at the URL in our own sources list) names Schadewald and block-quotes him at length: "Regardless, an online article, titled 'The Flat-Earth Bible,' written by Robert J. Schadewald, (c) 1987, 1995, states some things worth quoting here (I recommend you actually read the entire article too):" — followed by roughly five to six paragraphs of Schadewald, including "The vault of heaven is a crucial concept" and the NEB Isaiah 40:22 rendering "sits throned on the vaulted roof of earth", and carrying Job 37:18, Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 19:1, Psalm 102:25, Job 9:8, Job 22:14, Isaiah 42:5, 44:24, 45:12, 48:13 inside the quoted block. This is the same failure class as corrections.json entries 3, 8 and 9 (attribution asserted from the shape of the genre rather than checked against the primary text) running in the negative direction: we disclaimed a derivation that the primary source documents in plain sight. On a page whose product is provenance, throwing away a signed, dated, openly credited transmission is the most damaging error available. Note the finding is not plagiarism — Skiba credits Schadewald by name and tells readers to go read the whole article — and the replacement must say so.
_b7_C04.py.recommendation: Replace the sentence We do not claim Skiba took it from Schadewald, and we have no evidence that he did. What is established is that the list predates his teaching by twenty-eight years and that its first modern compiler was a debunker. with: Skiba takes it from Schadewald, and says so. The teaching document quoted above introduces “an online article, titled ‘The Flat-Earth Bible,’ written by Robert J. Schadewald, © 1987, 1995”, block-quotes several paragraphs of it, and tells the reader “I recommend you actually read the entire article too”. Job 37:18, Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 19:1, Job 9:8 and Isaiah 44:24 all reach the page inside that quotation. This is not concealment and nothing here suggests it was: the citation is open, credited and dated. It is something rarer and more useful — a fully documented link in a transmission chain, in which a distributor's proof-text set is lifted, with attribution, from a critic who assembled it to argue the opposite.

_b7_C04.py.quoted_phrase: endorses Augustine's reading of the firmament as the region of the air where clouds gather, calling it
_b7_C04.py.description: Misattributed quotation. The words "worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved" are Augustine's, not Aquinas's. Summa Theologiae I q.68 a.1 reads: "Augustine, in fact (Gen. ad lit. ii, 4), recommends it thus: 'I consider this view of the question worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved and believed.'" Aquinas is reporting Augustine's self-commendation, and in the body of the article he canvasses both the starry-heaven and the atmospheric readings under Augustine's rule about not adhering too firmly to any one of them — "endorses" is stronger than the article supports. We also silently truncate the quotation ("and believed" dropped without ellipsis). A defender with a copy of the Summa gets a free hit here, and it is precisely the citation-attribution error class that fills corrections.json.
_b7_C04.py.recommendation: Replace with: Aquinas, canvassing the opinions in Summa Theologiae I q.68 a.1, sets the starry-heaven reading beside Augustine's reading of the firmament as the region of the air where clouds gather, and records that “Augustine, in fact, recommends it thus: ‘I consider this view of the question worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved and believed’” — working throughout under Augustine's rule that one should hold a particular explanation “only in such measure as to be ready to abandon it, if it be proved with certainty to be false.” He does not settle the question; that a thirteenth-century doctor could leave it open is itself the point.

_b7_C07.py.quoted_phrase: every authority in the dossier held that the Earth is a sphere
_b7_C07.py.description: This is the topic sentence of `why_it_doesnt_save_claim` and the load-bearing claim of the whole entry, and it is stated at a strength that our own cited sources contradict on two counts. (1) Basil of Caesarea is the first authority the steelman leads with, and our own source entry five - Hexaemeron Homily 9 §1, newadvent.org/fathers/32019.htm - records that he declines to settle the Earth's shape: verified verbatim this pass, "If it be spherical or cylindrical, if it resemble a disc and is equally rounded in all parts, or if it has the for[m] of a winnowing basket and is hollow in the middle". An authority in our own dossier who explicitly refuses to say the Earth is a sphere is a counterexample to "every", and we cite him in the sources list without ever using him. (2) The sentence also drops the source's own hedge. Sungenis's claim, quoted verbatim in our own passage block, is scoped: "Every other Father who wrote at length on cosmological issues stated his belief... that the Earth was a sphere" - other than Lactantius, and restricted to those who wrote at length on cosmology. Our restatement is unqualified and universal. Refuting a fragment is the failure the hedge rule names; overstating a source in our own favour is the same failure with the sign flipped, and it is the single sentence a well-informed defender attacks first.
_b7_C07.py.recommendation:
Replace with: `every Father in the source's own sphericity dossier — and, at the strength he states it, every Father who wrote at length on cosmological issues — held that the Earth is a sphere`. Then append to the end of that paragraph: `

Basil is the instructive exception and it costs the argument nothing to say so: in Hexaemeron IX.1 he declines to settle the shape at all — “If it be spherical or cylindrical, if it resemble a disc … or if it has the form of a winnowing basket and is hollow in the middle” — on the ground that Scripture does not address it. He is a witness for a central and stationary Earth and an abstainer on its shape. Nobody in the dossier is a witness for a flat one.

`

_b6_D06.py.quoted_phrase: in both the Arabic and the Latin the correspondence clause is
_b6_D06.py.description: The TLDR says that in BOTH recensions the correspondence clause is subordinate to a purpose clause 'to accomplish the miracles of the one thing', and that 'the text closes by saying it has finished speaking about the operation of Sol'. Neither is true of the Arabic. The literal translation of the Kitab sirr al-khaliqa version (Wikipedia, Emerald Tablet) reads 'indeed, the uppermost is from the lowermost and the lowermost is from the uppermost, / [it] worked the wonders from one, (just) as all things come from one by means of one plan' — a coordinate past-tense declarative, not a purpose construction — and it closes 'this is my renown and therefore I am named Hermes the threefold with the wisdom.' The gerundive 'ad preparanda miracula rei unius' and the closing 'Completum est quod diximus de opere solis' are peculiar to the Latin vulgate. Our own refutation §1 makes exactly this distinction ('the comparison is peculiar to the translation'); the TLDR then collapses it. This is the entry's headline sentence, the field readers see first and may never expand past, and it attributes to a primary source a grammatical structure and a closing line the source does not have — the same failure class the hedge rule exists to catch, run inward on our own body text.
_b6_D06.py.recommendation: Replace with: "The maxim is the licence for an alchemical operation, not a description of the sky. In the Latin vulgate the correspondence clause is subordinate to a purpose clause — ad preparanda miracula rei unius, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing — and that version signs off by saying it has finished speaking about the operation of Sol. The older Arabic does not compare the two realms at all: it derives one from the other, and says the wonders were worked from one."

Item 161 in scripts/corpus.py reads, in full: 'Hermetic as above so below.' The Kybalion ch. II reads 'As above, so below; as below, so above.' (verified verbatim, sacred-texts kyb04 and Gutenberg #14209). Worse, the compression block quotes the true item text in its own list_phrasing field four lines above the sentence that contradicts it, so the error is self-demonstrating to any reader of that block.
_b6_D06.py.recommendation: In §3 replace with: "item 161 is its axiom in compressed form — the Kybalion's doubled 'As above, so below; as below, so above.' arrives on the list as the bare 'Hermetic as above so below.' — and in chapter V it says:" In §2 replace 'in the form item 161 reproduces' with 'in the doubled form that item 161 compresses'. What changes far more than the words is what the sentence is taken to be about."

_b7_E13.py.quoted_phrase: every measurement here is of objects between 300 Mpc and the surface of last scattering
_b7_E13.py.description: The closing sweep asserts a distance floor our own section 5 breaks. Stiskalek, Desmond and Lavaux (MNRAS 546(2), staf2048, 22 January 2026), which section 5 relies on and concedes in full, restricts every sample to z<0.05 - CosmicFlows-4 Tully-Fisher W1 at z_CMB<~0.05, 2MTF at z_CMB<~0.03, SFI++ at z_CMB<~0.05, Pantheon+ at z_CMB<=0.05. That is roughly 200 Mpc and less. So the one item in the cluster where we concede a real directional detection is a measurement of objects entirely inside the radius we have just told the reader nothing here goes inside, and a defender answers our summary paragraph with our own strongest concession.
_b7_E13.py.recommendation: Ask what any of this would distinguish. Not one item separates a flat, stationary Earth from an ordinary spinning globe. The objects run from spiral galaxies a few tens of Mpc away, in the Tully–Fisher samples, out to the surface of last scattering, and every measurement of them is equally available on either account.

_b7_E13.py.quoted_phrase: which is what happens when a vocabulary is swept rather than an argument followed
_b7_E13.py.description: The refutation's final clause states as established fact a claim about how the list was produced. A critic putting the two side by side gets a self-contradiction inside one entry, and the version asserted without qualification is an unsupported claim about the working method of a named living compiler, which our own rules put in the escalate tier. people.py.description: False against the edition we link in this record's own sources[]. The 3rd ed. General Index (sacred-texts za68.htm) carries “Stars, north and south, motion of [284]” and “Southern Cross [287]”. The section itself (za48.htm, heading “Motion of Stars North and South”) argues that “all the constellations of the south—pole star included—sweep over a great southern arc and across the meridian”, states flatly that “there is no southern pole, no south pole star, and no southern circumpolar constellations”, cites Sir James Clark Ross, von Spix and von Martius, and Humboldt by name on their first-sighting latitudes for the Southern Cross, and discounts contrary reports on the ground that observers “educated to believe that the earth is a globe … do not examine such matters critically”. He engaged it for pages. This is the single first move available to a well-informed defender, and it is fatal to a project whose product is 'we went and read the primary text' — we missed something listed in the book's index. It also breaks the biography rule that `ignored` must mean data available and not engaged.
people.py.recommendation: He engaged it, and disqualified it. The 3rd edition's own General Index lists “Stars, north and south, motion of [284]” and “Southern Cross [287]”; in that section he denies that any southern pole, south pole star or southern circumpolar constellation exists, explains the Southern Cross away as a constellation that has simply not yet risen, and sets aside the reports of Ross, Humboldt and von Spix and von Martius on the ground that observers “educated to believe that the earth is a globe … do not examine such matters critically.” The failure is not that he never looked south. It is that when the observation could only come out one way, the observers stopped counting as witnesses.

people.py.quoted_phrase: First, atmospheric refraction over water — described in the surveying literature he was quoting from, and the reason a near-water sightline over a canal is the single worst configuration in which to test for curvature.
people.py.description: Filing refraction under `ignored` contradicts the primary text and our own ARG-B04. Rowbotham's General Index (za68.htm) has “Experiments showing that refraction does not account for the elevation of objects seen at a distance of several miles [31]-36” and “Refraction can only exist where the line of sight passes from one medium into another of different density [34]” — he ran experiments on it and stated a doctrine about it. scripts/_b6_B04.py says so in our own words: he “concedes refraction outright, quantifies it, applies it, and shows his working on Cape Bonavista”, deducting 13 feet by a one-twelfth-of-target-height rule. He did not ignore refraction; he underrated it and applied it to the wrong variable (refraction scales with the square of distance, not with target height), while reprinting the Encyclopædia Britannica coefficient — “about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth” — that would have given roughly five times more. As written, the field is both wrong and weaker than the true version.
people.py.recommendation: First, atmospheric refraction over water — which he underrated rather than overlooked. He reprints the Encyclopædia Britannica “Levelling” article, which gives him the mechanism and the coefficient (“at a mean … about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth”), and then substitutes an allowance of his own, one-twelfth of the target's height — the wrong variable, since refraction scales with the square of the distance and not with the height of the object. Elsewhere he denies the mechanism outright: “refraction can only exist where the line of sight passes from one medium into another of different density” (3rd ed., p. 34), which the article he had just typeset contradicts. The consequence is that he tested for curvature in the one configuration — a sightline a few inches above still water — where the effect he had cut by a factor of five is largest.

people.py.quoted_phrase: and over stellar aberration, which exists at all only because the Earth moves
people.py.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `ignored`. This says van der Kamp passed over stellar aberration. He did the opposite: De Labore Solis: Airy's Failure Reconsidered (1988) — the sole entry in his works[] and the work whose title we put on his card — is a book-length treatment of stellar aberration. It walks through Bradley and Molyneux at the chimney stack (p. 27), builds the whole argument on the aberration angle ('If the angle in this manner obtained is larger than the one measured by Bradley, the Earth indeed orbits... If no different value is registered, then the starry sphere swings', p. 29), and endorses the Boscovich water-telescope test as the decisive way to settle it. He kept the phenomenon and relocated the motion. The field renders under the heading 'The data they had, and passed over — Available to them, and not engaged. This is the difference between being wrong and being unserious', i.e. we are calling him unserious about the one topic he wrote a book on. And render.py prints 'Arguments originating here' on the same card, which for this person includes ARG-A04 'Stellar aberration is optical/parallax, not Earth's motion'. A defender needs one click to show the card contradicting itself.
people.py.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "He also passed over Michelson–Gale–Pearson (1925), a positive detection of the Earth's rotation published in the Astrophysical Journal — it appears neither in De Labore Solis nor in his later Biblical Astronomer restatement. Stellar aberration he did not pass over: De Labore Solis is a book about it. What he passed over is what aberration is evidence of. He kept Bradley's phenomenon and moved the motion — then the starry sphere swings — and never accounted for why the swing should imitate the Earth's orbit so exactly. His own successor declined to follow him there: Bouw rebuilt the model to keep aberration."

people.py.quoted_phrase: Bouw's obituary of him credits the coinage by name

Bouw is using the phrase as settled vocabulary and crediting the work, not the word.
